# Turkish and Morphologically Rich Languages {#sec-turkish-nlp}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** The measurements new to this chapter were run on
the WMT16/17/18 Turkish–English test sets — 9,007 professionally translated
sentence pairs, which give the same content in two languages and so allow
comparisons the usual monolingual corpora cannot. Where a number was measured
in an earlier chapter it is cited rather than repeated. To reproduce a table,
record the year, the language side, the sentence selection, the tokenization
and the tool version it used. Software:
`sacrebleu` 2.6.0, `snowballstemmer` 3.1.1, `transformers` 5.15.1, PyTorch
2.13.0 on Python 3.14.5.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- explain what agglutination does to vocabulary size, and show the effect on
  a corpus rather than asserting it;
- say which assumptions of an NLP pipeline need testing in a morphologically
  rich language, and check them in order;
- normalize Turkish text without destroying it, and name the two bugs that
  easily slip through code review;
- compare multilingual and monolingual models by measuring them on your own
  task data;
- recognise the general pattern this book has hit repeatedly: a standard tool
  that is silently wrong outside English, and the kind of control that catches
  it.

## What agglutination actually costs {#sec-turkish-nlp-agglutination}

Turkish is [**agglutinative**](#gloss-agglutinative){#term-agglutinative .term-ref}:
many inflectional and derivational meanings are expressed by morphemes added
to a stem. Their order and sound shape are constrained by rule — though a
suffix does not always carry exactly one feature and some do not take part in
vowel harmony — and most suffixes have vowels that harmonise with the stem — [**vowel harmony**](#gloss-vowel-harmony){#term-vowel-harmony .term-ref},
which is why the same suffix surfaces as *-ler* or *-lar*.

::: {#gloss-agglutinative .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Agglutinative** — a language that builds words by concatenating suffixes
that each carry one piece of grammar, rather than by fusing them or by using
separate words. Turkish, Finnish and Hungarian; that productivity is why
surface forms keep growing as the corpus grows. [↩](#term-agglutinative){.term-back}
:::

::: {#gloss-vowel-harmony .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Vowel harmony** — the rule that a suffix's vowels agree with the stem's last
vowel in *backness*, and — for four-way suffixes — in *rounding* as well, so one
suffix has two or four surface forms (*evler* but *kitaplar*; *evim*, *kitabım*,
*okulum*, *gözüm*). It multiplies the number of distinct strings a tokenizer
must account for. [↩](#term-vowel-harmony){.term-back}
:::

*Ev* is house; *evler* houses; *evlerimiz* our houses; *evlerimizden* from our
houses. One Turkish word, four morphemes — the stem plus plural, possessive and
case — where a likely English rendering, *from our houses*, is three words.

Measuring what that does to the number of surface forms in a corpus needs a
corpus where both languages say the same thing — which is exactly what a
professional translation is.

### Vocabulary growth, on identical content

So take one. Nine thousand news sentences, translated by professionals, and
count the distinct word forms on each side:

```text
WMT16/17/18 tr-en, 9,007 aligned sentence pairs

  Turkish   141,412 tokens   32,866 distinct forms
  English   182,429 tokens   16,652 distinct forms
```

[Over all 9,007 pairs, Turkish produces twice the vocabulary from 78% of the
tokens.]{.hl} Same content, same facts, same news stories. The table below
compares form counts after an *equal number of tokens* has been read in each
language; those points do not represent the same number of parallel sentences,
so the "same content" conclusion belongs to the full pair totals only. The
ratio is not fixed — over this range it grows with the corpus:

```text
   tokens seen     TR forms    EN forms    ratio
         5,000        2,471       1,655     1.49
        10,000        4,192       2,575     1.63
        25,000        9,342       5,016     1.86
        50,000       15,963       7,827     2.04
       100,000       25,664      11,848     2.17
       141,412       32,866      14,251     2.31
```

Those six rows are two curves. Both look consistent with Heaps' law (@sec-text-as-data-heaps) and both bend; they differ in how fast:

::: {.fig-cap}
Both curves are counted at equal token counts, so the gap is not an artefact of
one language needing more words to say the same thing — though equal token
prefixes do not cover the same sentences. Both curves bend, English faster: a
rough Heaps exponent from the six points' log-log slope is about 0.78 for
Turkish and about 0.65 for English (fit range and uncertainty not reported).
Over this corpus range the multiple between them is still growing.
:::
::::

On equal token prefixes the Turkish/English form ratio rises from 1.49 to
2.31. Neither language saturates — even the English side adds 2,401 new forms
between 141k and 182k tokens; English is productive too. But over this corpus
range **the Turkish curve rises faster**. The result holds for these news texts
and this tokenization; it does not show that the two exponents keep diverging,
and a larger corpus needs measuring separately. On the Turkish side about 870
new forms still arrive per 5,000 tokens between 100k and 141k. (Both exponents
sit above the typical 0.4–0.6 range given in @sec-text-as-data-heaps; in a corpus
this small the steep start of the curve pulls the slope up. What matters is the
difference between the languages.) Productive morphology makes a vocabulary
hard to represent as a fixed list.

The tail shows something similar — here, the share of each language's distinct
forms that occur exactly once:

```text
  forms occurring exactly once     Turkish   58.6%      English   44.1%
```

::: {.column-margin}
A form that occurs exactly once is called a *hapax* (plural *hapax
legomena*). @sec-bake-off measured 58.6% hapax on a completely different
Turkish corpus — product reviews rather than news, and six times larger — and
@sec-embeddings 50.0% on Turkish Wikipedia. Treat the exact match as a
coincidence: the hapax share depends on corpus length, domain, spelling and
tokenization. In these three measurements Turkish sat at or above half, well
over the 44.1% of English news above; do not treat that as a fixed property of
the language.
:::

### One stem, many words

Vocabulary size is one view of the cost. The other is what sits behind it —
how many of those distinct forms are the same word wearing different suffixes.
Stemming the corpus with Snowball and counting the forms under each stemming
key (a stemming key is not a linguistic lemma; it can merge different words and
split forms of the same lemma):

```text
  32,866 distinct forms  ->  17,891 stems       mean 1.84 forms per stem

  arkadaş   39 forms   arkadaş, arkadaşı, arkadaşım, arkadaşın, arkadaştı, ...
  ülke      35 forms   ülke, ülkem, ülkede, ülkeyi, ülkeye, ülkeden, ülkeler, ...
  el        34 forms   el, eli, ele, elim, elde, elin, elimi, ...
  çocuk     31 forms   çocuk, çocuğu, çocuğa, çocukla, çocuğun, çocukta, ...
```

The mean of 1.84 understates the effect, for two reasons. Most stems in a
corpus this small appear exactly once, which drags the mean towards 1
regardless of the language. And the stemmer under-merges wherever the stem
changes shape in a way its rules do not undo (rule 4 below), so some forms of
one word are counted under two stems. The informative row is the
top: **thirty-nine forms under the key *arkadaş* in 141,000 tokens** — an
observation about this corpus and this algorithm, not the same thing as the
number of forms per real lemma. @sec-bake-off, on a larger corpus, found 895
forms sharing the stem *kulla*.

### The rules behind the forms

Four facts are major sources of surface-form variety in Turkish noun
inflection, and all four are already at work in the list above (verb
inflection, derivation and compounds bring further rules). Naming them matters here, because the fourth is
exactly where the stemmers later in this chapter go wrong.

**1. Suffix order is fixed.** In the standard productive pattern a Turkish noun
is `STEM (+PLURAL) (+POSSESSIVE) (+CASE) (+CLITIC)`, and that order does not
vary: *ev-ler-imiz-den*, never \**ev-den-ler-imiz*. (Derivational suffixes and
compounds complicate the picture — a derived stem can itself carry inflection —
but the inflectional slots keep this sequence. One notable exception is *-ki*,
which renominalises an inflected noun and restarts the plural–possessive–case
cycle: *ev-de-ki-ler-in*, even *evdekilerinki*.)

**2. Backness harmony (*büyük ünlü uyumu*)** gives two-way suffixes: the plural
*-lAr* surfaces as *-ler* after a front vowel (*ev-ler*) and *-lar* after a back
one (*kitap-lar*).

**3. Rounding harmony (*küçük ünlü uyumu*)**, layered on backness harmony, gives four-way suffixes: the
first-person possessive *-Im* surfaces as *-im* (*ev-im*), *-ım* (*kitab-ım*),
*-um* (*okul-um*) and *-üm* (*göz-üm*). This is the rule that multiplies forms
fastest, and it is the one the usual one-sentence summary of vowel harmony
leaves out.

Both harmony rules have exceptions, and a morphological analyser has to model
them explicitly: some suffixes' vowels do not harmonise (*-yor*, *-ken*, *-ki*,
*-leyin*: *geliyor*, *okurken*, *evdeki*, *sabahleyin*), and in some loanwords
and historical forms the suffix does not follow the stem's last vowel
(*saat-ler*, *rol-ü*, *kalp-ler*). A subword tokenizer, by contrast, does not
have to find morpheme boundaries; its segmentation quality is measured
separately.

**4. Sounds change on both sides of the seam.** In many words the last consonant of the
stem becomes voiced before a vowel (*kitap* → *kitab-ı*, *çocuk* → *çocuğ-u*; but *top* → *top-u*), the first
consonant of the suffix loses its voicing after a voiceless consonant (*arkadaş* + *-(y)DI* → *arkadaş-tı*),
a buffer consonant is inserted between two vowels (*ülke* + *-I* →
*ülke-y-i*), and in some words the last vowel of the stem drops out (*ağız* →
*ağz-ı*, *burun* → *burn-u*). None of these is a different suffix: it is the
same stem, or the same suffix, changing shape.

Rule 4 is the one that troubles stemmers most. **The stem is not constant**, so
plain suffix stripping can miss pairs with a sound change such as *kitap* and
*kitabı*. In retrieval that can make a query miss a relevant document; measure
the effect at the document and query level. The
Snowball Turkish stemmer used in this chapter patches the commonest case: after
stripping, it turns a final *b*, *c*, *d* or *ğ* back into *p*, *ç*, *t* or
*k*, which is why *çocuğu* sits under *çocuk* in the list above and *kitabı*
stems to *kitap*. The other changes it does not undo: *ağzı* and *burnu* stay
apart from *ağız* and *burun*, and *rengi* from *renk*.

### Where this shows up

Agglutination is not one problem; it is the same problem arriving in four
places. The last row comes from a second Turkish peculiarity independent of
agglutination — the alphabet (agglutinative Finnish does not have it) — but it
breaks the same pipelines. This book has now measured each of them:

| where | what happens | measured in |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Tokenization | with an English-centric tokenizer, more tokens for the same content, so more cost and less effective context | @sec-pretraining |
| Vocabulary | twice the types and a longer tail in this corpus; an out-of-vocabulary rate needs a defined vocabulary and test set | here |
| Lexical retrieval | a query form that differs from the document form matches nothing | @sec-turkish-nlp-retrieval |
| Word-level metrics | fewer tokens per sentence; metrics can be sensitive to Turkish suffix changes (exploratory, no firm penalty factor) | @sec-machine-translation |
| Case folding | one character breaks the whole pipeline | @sec-turkish-nlp-normalization |

: Five Turkish traps: four from agglutination, one from the alphabet {tbl-colwidths="[22,52,26]"}

**What we will look at.** First normalization, where the default
implementation of two steps can give wrong results on Turkish and easily slips
through code review because the code looks right. Then morphological analysis, which subword tokenizers mostly
replaced, and the four jobs it is still the right tool for. Then search, where
one preprocessing step moves recall@1 from 28% to 95%. Then the pattern this
book keeps walking into — a standard tool, silently wrong outside English,
caught by a control rather than by reading its source. Then a short map of
Turkish corpora, models and benchmarks. And finally monolingual against
multilingual, examined by running both.

## Turkish normalization, and the two bugs that survive review {#sec-turkish-nlp-normalization}

Normalization is a task-dependent decision in every language. In Turkish, the
default implementation of two steps — locale-independent lowercasing and blind
stripping of Turkish letters to ASCII — loses distinctions on some inputs, and
both are easy to miss in code review because the code looks right.

### Bug one: `str.lower()` is wrong in both directions

Turkish has two letters where English has one — the
[**dotted and dotless i**](#gloss-dotted-and-dotless-i){#term-dotted-and-dotless-i .term-ref}.
Dotted `İ`/`i` and dotless
`I`/`ı` are different letters with different sounds, and the case mapping
between them is not the ASCII one:

```text
        Unicode default        Turkish locale
  I  →  i                      ı
  İ  →  i + combining dot      i
```

::: {#gloss-dotted-and-dotless-i .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Dotted and dotless i** — Turkish has two i letters where English has one: dotted `i`/`İ` and dotless `ı`/`I`. They are distinct letters, so case conversion between them does not follow the ASCII rule, and `str.lower()` gets both capitals wrong: `I` becomes `i` instead of `ı`, and `İ` becomes `i` plus a combining dot. [↩](#term-dotted-and-dotless-i){.term-back}
:::

Python's `str.lower()` and JavaScript's `toLowerCase()` apply the
locale-independent Unicode default mapping — the "Unicode default" above; not an
English-specific rule, but not the output Turkish I/İ needs. Java's argument-less `toLowerCase()` and .NET's `ToLower()` use the active
locale or culture, so the same code can give one result on a Turkish-locale
laptop and another on the server (the classic "Turkish I" bug: `"TITLE"`
becomes `"tıtle"`). In production, set the locale explicitly for Turkish text,
and in tests compare the `tr-TR` and invariant-locale results.
On the WMT16 Turkish source:

```text
  tokens in the WMT16 Turkish source                      46,243
  tokens containing I or İ                                   438   (0.95%)
  of those, where str.lower() differs from Turkish rules     438   (100%, by construction)

    'İtiraf'      str.lower() 'i̇tiraf'       Turkish 'itiraf'
    'İngilizce'   str.lower() 'i̇ngilizce'    Turkish 'ingilizce'
    'İşlerin'     str.lower() 'i̇şlerin'      Turkish 'işlerin'
```

**The 100% is not a finding.** The two case mappings differ for both letters —
`I` goes to `ı` in Turkish and `i` in English, `İ` goes to `i` in Turkish and
`i` plus a combining dot in English — so *every* token containing either letter
must come out different. It is arithmetic, and reporting it as a measurement
would be the kind of thing this book keeps telling you to check for.

The finding is the **0.95%**: in this WMT16 source, one token in a hundred
comes out different from the Turkish mapping under locale-independent
lowercasing. A capital dotted İ would be expected to cluster in proper nouns and
sentence-initial words starting with *i* — tokens a retrieval or NER system
cares about — but we did not count those subgroups; measure the effect on task
errors separately.

::: {.anlp-widget}
```{=html}
<div class="widget-title">Lowercase it yourself — English rules against Turkish rules</div>
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof trCaseInput = Inputs.text({
  label: "Turkish text",
  value: "İSTANBUL İtiraf IŞIK Iğdır",
  width: 420,
  placeholder: "try: İzmir, IRMAK, İŞLERİN, KIZILAY"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
trCaseRows = trCaseInput.split(/\s+/).filter(w => w.length > 0).map(w => {
  const naive = w.toLowerCase();                  // what str.lower() does
  const proper = w.toLocaleLowerCase("tr");       // locale-aware, the fix
  return {
    word: w,
    naive: naive,
    proper: proper,
    agree: naive === proper,
    // a combining mark is not a \w character, so it splits the token in two
    pieces: naive.normalize("NFC").split(/[^\p{L}\p{N}]+/u).filter(x => x).length
  };
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Inputs.table(trCaseRows, {
  columns: ["word", "naive", "proper", "agree", "pieces"],
  header: {word: "input", naive: "str.lower()", proper: "Turkish lower()",
           agree: "same?", pieces: "pieces after JS letter/digit split"},
  format: {agree: a => a ? "yes" : "NO", pieces: n => n > 1 ? `${n} ⚠` : `${n}`},
  width: {word: 130, naive: 150, proper: 150, agree: 70, pieces: 110},
  rows: 12})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`${trCaseRows.filter(r => !r.agree).length} of ${trCaseRows.length} words
lowercase differently under the two rules${
trCaseRows.some(r => r.pieces > 1)
  ? ", and at least one no longer survives tokenization as a single word"
  : ""}. This interactive example is not an exact implementation of Python's
\`re.findall(r"\\w+", …)\`; it shows a similar split at the combining dot.`
```
:::

Your browser has the correct mapping built in — `toLocaleLowerCase("tr")` —
and so do Java, .NET and ICU; Python's standard library does not (see below). The bug is never that the fix is
unavailable; it is that the default is wrong and silent.

### Bug two: the result is not even one word any more

The first bug is a wrong string. The second is worse, and it is the one
@sec-clustering found in real data:

```text
  'İSTANBUL'.lower()  =  'i̇stanbul'

    code points  U+0069 U+0307 U+0073 U+0074 U+0061 U+006E U+0062 U+0075 U+006C
                   i     ̇      s      t      a      n      b      u      l
    categories   Ll     Mn     Ll     Ll     Ll     Ll     Ll     Ll     Ll

  re.findall(r"\w+", 'İSTANBUL'.lower())   →   ['i', 'stanbul']
```

`U+0307 COMBINING DOT ABOVE` is a *nonspacing mark*, and Python's `re` does not
count it as a word character, so a tokenizer built on `\w+` splits the word in
two at that point. Check your own engine before assuming it behaves the same
way: `\w` is defined per implementation, and some engines fold nonspacing marks
into it while others do not.
[`İstanbul` becomes `i` plus `stanbul`]{.hl}; pre-tokenization like that can
break the word's identity and affect later retrieval or tagging steps. The
effect depends on the model and features used (a subword model may handle it
differently), so test it in your own pipeline.

And it does not go away when you normalize:

```text
  s = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", 'İSTANBUL'.lower())    # still 'i̇stanbul'
  re.findall(r"\w+", s)                                  →   ['i', 'stanbul']
  re.findall(r"\w+", 'TAVSİYE'.lower())                  →   ['tavsi', 'ye']
```

NFC does not recombine, because NFC only composes a sequence into a single
code point when such a code point exists, and none exists for `i` + combining
dot. There is no fix at the level of Unicode normalization; the fix is a
library that applies Unicode's language-specific casing rules (the Turkish and
Azeri conditions in `SpecialCasing.txt`), such as ICU.

There is no standard-library fix either, and the folk answer is wrong: `str.casefold()`
is not locale-aware, and on `TAVSİYE` it produces the identical eight codepoints
that `lower()` does, combining dot included. A reader who reaches for it because
"casefold is the more correct lowercasing" gets exactly the bug they were trying
to avoid. Python has no Turkish casing at all; ICU does
(`PyICU`, `icu.UnicodeString(s).toLower(icu.Locale("tr"))`). For most pipelines
the cheaper answer is to not create the problem:

```python
import unicodedata

def tr_lower(s):
    # NFC first: a decomposed İ (I + U+0307) has to become the precomposed
    # character, or the replace below misses it and the combining mark survives.
    s = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", s)
    return s.replace("İ", "i").replace("I", "ı").lower()

def tr_upper(s):
    s = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", s)
    return s.replace("i", "İ").replace("ı", "I").upper()
```

Two small functions, applied before anything else touches the text — and the
NFC line is not optional. They are a practical start for the common composed
and decomposed I/İ cases in Turkish text; for general Unicode case conversion
use ICU with the Turkish locale, and test the helpers separately on text with
combining marks, mixed languages and edge cases. Text arrives decomposed more often than you would like: from HTML
forms, from some macOS filenames, from OCR. Without the normalization,
`tr_lower` on a decomposed `İstanbul` returns `ı̇stanbul` — the combining dot is
still there and it is now over the *wrong* vowel, which is worse than what you
started with.

::: {.column-margin}
This is why the bug survives: the code that causes it is `text.lower()`, which
is correct-looking, ubiquitous, and inside every library you did not write.
In @sec-clustering it became visible because a cluster came back 94.7% full of
one artefact, and reading that cluster identified it — nobody had set out to
look for it. A cluster like that is a warning; confirming the cause means
comparing those documents' lowercased code points and tokens with the raw
text. In your own pipeline, check by lowercasing a word with `İ` and printing
the code points.
:::

### Diacritics: deasciification and what it merges

Turkish keyboards are not universal, and input with Turkish letters typed as
their ASCII look-alikes is common in some products — *guzel* for *güzel*, *cok*
for *çok*; measure the share in your own data. Handling it means restoring the
letters
([**deasciification**](#gloss-deasciification){#term-deasciification .term-ref}),
stripping them everywhere so both forms match, or keeping the original and
adding a secondary ASCII matching channel.

::: {#gloss-deasciification .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Deasciification** — restoring Turkish diacritics to text typed without
them (*guzel* → *güzel*). The inverse, stripping diacritics so both forms
match, is easier and merges word pairs that are genuinely different.
[↩](#term-deasciification){.term-back}
:::

Stripping is the tempting one-liner. Measured on the same corpus:

```text
  words containing a Turkish-specific character   19,318 / 46,243   (41.8%)
  distinct forms                                          15,173
  distinct forms after stripping diacritics               15,101
  ascii forms now ambiguous between 2+ real words             72

     'oldu'   <-  oldu, öldü          (it happened / he died)
     'bas'    <-  bas, baş            (press / head)
     'sac'    <-  saç, sac            (hair / sheet metal)
     'yasa'   <-  yasa, yaşa          (law / live!)
```

The distinct-form count fell from 15,173 to 15,101, a net loss of 72 forms; the
ASCII keys standing for at least two original forms also number 72 (the two
counts agree only if every key merges exactly two forms). Only 72 collisions,
which sounds harmless until you read them. *Oldu* and
*öldü* are "it happened" and "he died". Not every merge in that list of 72
costs something, and it is worth checking rather than counting: *mi* and *mı*
also collapse together, but they are the same question particle under vowel
harmony, so nothing is lost. [The merge rate is low, but some merges cost the
whole meaning]{.hl}, and they do not show up in aggregate metrics. Sample the
collision keys for your domain and measure how often the affected tokens occur
(72/15,173 is a share of forms, not of tokens).

Where possible, restore the letters with a context-aware method and measure its
error on your own data — a deasciifier can also insert the wrong letter. Ready
tools exist: Deniz Yüret's decision-list Turkish deasciifier (with Python and
JavaScript ports), Zemberek's noisy-text normalisation and the suggestions of
`trnlp` in the table below. Their accuracy varies with the kind of text, so
measure it on a few hundred hand-corrected words of your own. For retrieval,
also test keeping the original form and using ASCII matching as an extra search
channel. If you must strip, strip the *query* and the *document* both with the
same mapping, know that you have made those pairs indistinguishable, and track
false matches separately.

## Morphological analysis, and whether you still need it {#sec-turkish-nlp-analysis}

Before subword tokenizers, handling Turkish meant *analysing* it: taking
*evlerimizden* and returning the stem *ev* plus an ordered list of the
grammatical functions stacked on it. Turkish has one of the field's great
success stories here — @oflazer1994two built a two-level finite-state
analyser that relates dictionary forms to surface forms through phonological
and suffix rules, and its descendants still work. Its coverage is bounded by
its lexicon and rules, and choosing the right analysis in context is a separate
step (both come back below). ("Two-level" means the rules relate two strings directly: the
dictionary-level form, such as *kitap* + *-I*, and the surface form *kitabı*.
That is how an analyser undoes rule 4 above rather than stumbling over it.)

Two things make analysis harder than it sounds:

**Ambiguity.** *Yüzü* has at least four analyses: *yüz* "face" with the
third-person possessive (*his* or *her face*), *yüz* "face" with the accusative (*the
face*), and *yüz* "hundred" with either. (The difference between *yüz* "face" and *yüz*
"surface" is lexical, not morphological: a morphological analyser gives both
the same analysis, and telling them apart is a job for semantic tagging.) A
sharper case is *koyun*, which is at least three separate stems in one surface
form:
*koyun* "sheep", *koy* "bay" with a possessive (*your bay*) or genitive
(*of the bay*), and *koy-* "put" in the
second-person plural imperative. A morphological analyser returns every reading
its lexicon allows; the exact list varies from tool to tool, so check what
yours returns. Picking the right one is *morphological disambiguation*, and it needs
sentence context. So the tidy pipeline — analyse, then model — has a
sentence-level model inside its first step.

**Coverage.** An analyser knows the stems it was built with. New words and
derivations, brand names, loanwords, typos and slang strain it. If the tool
offers no guessing for unknown words, the failure is a hard one: no analysis at
all. Some tools do offer such a fallback; find out what yours does from its
documentation and your own tests.

**Stem or lemma.** @sec-text-as-data separated stemming (chopping endings off
to get a matching key) from lemmatization (returning the dictionary form). In
Turkish the gap between the two is wide. The Snowball stemmer's output need not
be a word — *burun* "nose" becomes *bur*, and *ağız* "mouth" becomes *ak*,
which is a different word ("white"). (In this book "stem" is meant in the NLP
sense, the stemmer's output, which can be a non-word like *bur* or collide with
another word like *ak*; do not confuse it with the grammatical stem, a root plus
its derivational suffixes.) It also targets the endings nouns take,
so verbs keep their tense and aspect: *okuyorlar* "they are reading" becomes
*okuyor*, and *gidiyor* "is going" comes back unchanged. A lemmatizer built on
an analyser, such as Zemberek's, returns *burun* for *burnu* and *git* for
*gidiyor* (the root; a Turkish dictionary's headword is *gitmek*, as in
@sec-text-as-data) — this root is usually what NLP tools return as the lemma,
but only after choosing among the readings, which is the ambiguity problem
above. Which output counts as the lemma depends on the tool and the dictionary
tradition, so say which one you mean when you compare two systems.

### So do you need it in 2026?

For many modelling tasks, usually not. Subword tokenization (@sec-subword)
handles morphology *statistically* rather than linguistically: it represents
words with frequent character-sequence pieces and does not mark morpheme
boundaries. It does not know that *-lerimizden* is three suffixes on a stem;
the sequence may be one piece or be split at points that do not line up with
the suffixes. The model still learns a great deal from recurring pieces and
context. That is why BERTurk does well on many tasks without a morphological
analyser anywhere in the stack. It does not follow that analysis never helps:
on tasks that need morphological tags or generated word forms, measure its
benefit separately.

Reach for a real analyser when you need something a subword model does not
give you:

- **Lexical retrieval**, where a stemmer is not enough: compare surface
  forms, Snowball stems and an analyser's root or lemma index on your own
  queries. @sec-turkish-nlp-retrieval compares surface forms with the stemmer
  and two simple fallbacks; an analyser index was not tried there.
- **Linguistic annotation**, where the grammatical analysis *is* the output.
- **Rule-driven products** — grammar checkers, spelling correction,
  dictionary lookup — where a wrong answer must be explainable.
- **Very low data regimes**, where the inductive bias of knowing that
  *evlerimizden* and *evimiz* share a stem is worth more than the data you do
  not have.

::: {.column-margin}
The compromise most projects land on is a stemmer rather than an analyser:
crude, fast, and with no ambiguity to resolve. The Snowball Turkish stemmer
used throughout this chapter is a few hundred lines of rules. It under-merges,
it over-merges, and in the experiment of @sec-turkish-nlp-retrieval it takes
recall@1 from 28.0% to 95.3%. Those queries were derived from the target
sentence with inflection differences kept deliberately high; the result is not
a general gain for every Turkish search task.
:::

## Turkish retrieval: how much of the gap is morphology {#sec-turkish-nlp-retrieval}

One well-known difficulty of Turkish lexical search is inflection: the form a
user types and the form in the document often differ. What is worth knowing is
*how much* of the difficulty comes from inflection differences alone — because
that part has a cheap fix. (No measurement comparing Turkish with English is
made here.)

The experiment isolates it. Take 7,165 Turkish sentences as documents, index
them with BM25 — the standard word-matching ranking function, which scores a
document by the query words it contains (@sec-text-as-data) — and query with three
content words drawn from a target document, but in a **different surface form
than the document uses**. The case being imitated: the user types *İstanbul*,
the document says *İstanbul'da*; but the queries were built from the target
document, not taken from a user log. Each query has one target document chosen
in advance. The score is recall@1, the share of queries whose target comes back
in first place (recall@10: anywhere in the top ten); it is not classic recall
over all relevant documents.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Setup.** Corpus: 7,165 sentences of 8+ words from the Turkish side of
WMT16–18, one document each. Query: three content words from the target
document; 69% of the terms are in a different inflection than the document's,
drawn from elsewhere in the corpus. Ranking: BM25 with four index/query
schemes. Success: the target document in first place (recall@1).
:::

```text
7,165 Turkish documents (sentences of 8+ words)
1,481 queries of 3 terms each
69% of query terms are a different inflection than the document uses

index / query scheme      recall@1   recall@10   terms/doc
surface form                 28.0%       54.4%        15.7
5-char prefix                74.6%       92.6%        15.7
Snowball stem                95.3%       99.8%        15.7
character 4-grams            74.9%       94.9%        55.7
```

[Surface-form BM25 finds the right document 28% of the time. Stemming takes
it to 95.3%.]{.hl} One preprocessing step, a 3.4× improvement, and no model
involved at all. That 3.4× holds for three-term queries chosen this way; real
user queries need their own measurement.

Read the setup before you take the headline anywhere, because three separate
things could inflate that 3.4× on their own.

**How the queries were made decides whether the number is circular.** If a
query term were produced by applying a suffix rule, the same rule-based stemmer
would be scored against its own inverse and 95.3% would be near-tautological.
The forms here are drawn from elsewhere in the corpus rather than generated,
which avoids that — but the design is still *known-item* retrieval: the query
comes from the target document, so this setup makes a stem match easy once
stemming works at all. Do not read 95.3% as an estimate of real user
performance or as a theoretical upper bound; measure it on a real query log.

**And part of the gain is string surgery rather than morphology.** Since
version 3.0.0, `snowballstemmer`'s Turkish algorithm truncates a token at its
first apostrophe (ignoring one in the first two characters, so *O'Neill'in*
keeps *O'Neill*), then goes on to stem what is left with the normal rules. So
in the chapter's own headline example, `İstanbul'da` → `İstanbul`, the work is
done by the truncation step rather than the morphological rules; a
`split("'")` would give the same result. On a news
corpus full of inflected proper nouns that step alone is worth a share of the
gap, and we did not separate it. Two rows would: apostrophe truncation with no
stemming, and Snowball with the apostrophe step disabled. They are the first
thing to run before quoting 3.4× anywhere. (One practical trap: only the ASCII
apostrophe `'` counts. The typographic `’`, common in edited text, is not
recognised. Replacing it with `'` before stemming is one fix, but `’` also
serves as a closing quotation mark, so check on your own data that the mapping
does not cause wrong truncations outside proper nouns.)

Finally, 69% of query terms were deliberately chosen to be a different
inflection, and a query can only rank its target first if enough of its three
terms match the indexed form. How inflection differences and query length are
distributed in real user queries was not measured here; users may type bare
forms, inflected forms, multi-word phrases or proper nouns. Whether this setup
is harsher or gentler than an average query can only be said after measuring
it on a query log.

Three practical consequences:

1. **Stemming is not optional in Turkish lexical search — on queries like
   these.** In English it is usually reported as a marginal tweak. Here it is
   the difference between a search box that works and one that does not. Keep
   the condition attached — the 69% above is what makes exact matching fail —
   and on a corpus whose users type the same forms the documents use, the gap
   shrinks. Measure it on your own query log before quoting this as a universal
   requirement.
2. **Character n-grams are the robust fallback.** 74.9% recall@1 with no
   linguistic knowledge at all, at the cost of 3.5× the terms per document
   (55.7 against 15.7). The index size in bytes depends on the posting lists
   and compression and was not measured here. When you have no stemmer for a
   language, this is the first fallback to try.
3. **Prefix truncation is a surprisingly good approximation.** Keeping the
   first five characters gets 74.6% — nearly the same as character n-grams,
   with no increase in terms per document. It is crude, it is wrong on short
   words, it can merge words that are not equivalent into one prefix and so
   produce false matches (false matches were not counted in this experiment),
   and it is what to reach for when a real stemmer is not available. Measure
   both prefix truncation and character n-grams on real queries for recall,
   false matches and storage in bytes.

::: {.column-margin}
This is also a reason to try dense retrieval in Turkish: because the model
learns forms from context rather than by matching strings, the dense
representations of *İstanbul'da* and *İstanbul* may be close in some models.
That was not measured in this setup; compare stemmed sparse, dense and hybrid
indexes on the same real query set. @sec-retrieval builds dense retrieval
properly, including the
*hybrid* retriever that combines a word-matching (sparse) half with an
embedding (dense) half. The measurement here says what the sparse half needs
on queries like these: stemming. Without it, that half does not pull its weight
here.
:::

## The five-chapter pattern {#sec-turkish-nlp-pattern}

Something has happened repeatedly in this book, and it is worth naming as a
pattern rather than leaving as a handful of anecdotes. In each case a common
tool, or a measurement we wrote ourselves, produced a silently misleading
number on Turkish, and in most cases a *control measurement* — not a better
model — is what exposed it. The six rows are not the same kind of thing: two
are locale-dependent lowercasing, one is train/test overlap, one is a metric's
tokenizer, one is an implementation bug in a proxy measure, and the last is a
difference in metric scale between two languages.

| chapter | the tool | what it did on Turkish | how it surfaced |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| @sec-bake-off | `str.lower()` | `IYI` → `iyi` under English rules, `ıyı` under Turkish | comparing the two case mappings side by side |
| @sec-clustering | `str.lower()` | `İ` becomes `i` + a combining mark, splitting the word | a cluster that was 94.7% one artefact |
| @sec-sequence-labeling | WikiANN | 13.06% of the test set sitting verbatim in training | hashing test inputs against training inputs |
| @sec-summarization | `rouge-score` | its tokenizer split 44.4% of the words in 300 Turkish references at Turkish letters | two implementations of one metric disagreeing |
| @sec-summarization | a faithfulness proxy | its buggy first version also flagged copied text, so the 56% it gave human journalists' summaries could not be interpreted | scoring copied text: this measure only looks at numbers and proper nouns missing from the source, so a verbatim copy must get zero flags |
| @sec-machine-translation | BLEU | about 22.5% fewer word tokens per sentence (English uses 29% more); a possible mechanism by which an error costs more in a word n-gram metric | two separate perturbations on unmatched subsets in two languages (exploratory; the direction of the bias cannot be stated) |

: Six different evaluation risks that surfaced in Turkish experiments, and the control that made each visible {tbl-colwidths="[20,14,38,28]"}

Three things generalise, and none of them is about Turkish specifically.

**The tools were not broken; they were untested outside their assumptions.**
`rouge-score` reproduces the original Perl behaviour faithfully. BLEU does
exactly what its definition says. WikiANN was built as described. Each is
correct on the language it was validated on, and each carries an assumption
its documentation does not state. (The faithfulness proxy is the exception: we
wrote it, and its flaw was a plain implementation bug.)

**Every one was caught by a control, not by inspection.** Two case mappings
side by side; a cluster that should not exist; test inputs hashed against
training; two implementations of one metric compared; copied text that must
get zero flags from this measure; one perturbation in each of two languages
(exploratory). [When you cannot verify a metric directly, feed it an input
whose correct answer you already know.]{.hl} In these examples, controls of
this kind are what made the problems visible. Reading the code could have
caught some of them too — a Unicode regex and a data split are both visible in
code — so the two methods complement each other rather than compete.

**The failures were silent by construction.** No exception, no warning, no
missing field — just a ROUGE-1 that was 22% to 80% higher than with the right
tokenizer (`rouge-score`'s default, on the six systems of @sec-summarization;
the size depends on the corpus, the system and the tokenizer), or a benchmark
whose test set was 13% verbatim training material. A pipeline that fails loudly is a pipeline you will fix. The
ones to worry about are the ones that return a plausible float.

::: {.column-margin}
If you work in a language that is not English, expect this and budget for it.
The practical version: before trusting any tool on your language, run it on a
few short inputs whose answer is known — I/İ, a combining mark, identical
strings, an empty output, a copied document, a one-word change that alters the
meaning — and check that the number is what it must be. Preparing these
usually does not take long; after that, audit more widely on your real data
and metric protocol.
:::

## Turkish corpora, models, and benchmarks {#sec-turkish-nlp-ecosystem}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
This section dates faster than anything else in the book. Treat the names as a
map of *kinds* of resource rather than a leaderboard, and check what is
current before committing to one.
:::

Knowing what to distrust is half the job. The other half is knowing what
exists, and there is more Turkish infrastructure than most people outside
Turkey assume.

**Encoders.** BERTurk [@schweter2020berturk] remains the default Turkish
encoder and is what @sec-sequence-labeling and @sec-classification fine-tuned.
It exists in cased and uncased variants, and for tasks where Turkish letters
matter the **cased** one is a strong candidate (the two were not compared in
this chapter). The uncased checkpoint's configuration only says "lowercase";
loaded with the library defaults, its tokenizer then lowercases with the
English rules (@sec-turkish-nlp-normalization) and, because accent stripping
is switched on by default whenever lowercasing is, also removes the
diacritics. `IŞIK` comes out as `isik`, and `öldü` as `oldu` — the merge the
diacritics section warns about — even though the model's vocabulary is full
of pieces containing `ş`, `ü` or `ç` that then never get used. Those pieces
suggest the pretraining text kept these letters, in which case
`strip_accents=False` with `tr_lower` applied first may be the consistent
setting. But that is an inference: if you use the uncased checkpoint, inspect
its saved tokenizer files and the documented pretraining preprocessing, do not
change the setting one-sidedly at inference time (the token ids change and may
no longer match the weights), and compare alternative settings after
fine-tuning on an independent test set.

A newer generation of encoders is appearing alongside BERTurk; for example,
Boğaziçi University's TabiBERT (2025), built on the ModernBERT architecture.
These names are example candidates, not a quality ranking. On the day you
choose, record each model's card, weight revision, training data, licence and
measurement on your target task; the comparison protocol below applies to
them unchanged.

**Multilingual encoders.** mBERT and XLM-R [@conneau2020unsupervised] cover
Turkish among a hundred other languages. @sec-turkish-nlp-decide measures what
that costs.

**Generative models.** The Turkish-specific generative landscape — TURNA,
Kanarya, Trendyol's and Cosmos's LLMs, and the Turkish-adapted Llama and
Qwen derivatives — changes every few months. What does not change is the
question to ask about each: *what was it trained on, and can you use it?*
Licence terms vary from model to model; read and record the licence on each
model's card on the day you choose. A model you cannot deploy commercially is
not a candidate for commercial work. Do not read these names as a quality
ranking either.

**Benchmarks.** Mukayese [@safaya2022mukayese] assembled Turkish baselines
across tasks precisely because the field kept reporting Turkish numbers that
could not be compared with each other. Turkish versions of the standard
benchmark suites also exist and are used. A few names to look up at the time
of writing: TurkishMMLU, compiled from Turkish exam questions, for multi-domain
general knowledge; for question answering, the Turkish part of XQuAD, translated
from English, and TQuAD, written in Turkish; and Cetvel and TurkBench as
combined suites for LLMs. The names will date, the kinds will not; the two
cautions below apply to each.

Two cautions about all of them, both of which this book has already
demonstrated on other corpora:

1. **Translation artefacts.** A benchmark translated from English still
   measures the task, but through text carried over into Turkish.
   Translationese can have different word order and sentence length, and
   vocabulary chosen by a translator or a translation system. Benchmarks
   written in Turkish and translated ones can differ in their linguistic
   properties, and both give limited information about task performance.
   Check whether the benchmark was written in Turkish or rendered into it.
2. **Contamination.** @sec-sequence-labeling found 13.06% of a standard
   Turkish NER benchmark's test set sitting verbatim in its own training set;
   1,305 of those also carried the same reference labels. Before you believe a
   score, report train/test exact-input overlap, label agreement on the
   overlapping inputs, and near-duplicates separately; a hash or exact
   comparison only catches exact copies. Pretraining exposure can be audited
   only if you have access to the model's pretraining data.

## Multilingual or monolingual: deciding with a measurement {#sec-turkish-nlp-decide}

The question arrives on every Turkish project, and it is usually answered by
preference. Here it is answered by running both.

`bert-base-multilingual-cased` and `dbmdz/bert-base-turkish-cased` are
comparable models — same architecture, same era, same fine-tuning recipe —
differing in what they were pretrained on. @sec-sequence-labeling's NER setup,
identical in every other respect, gives the comparison.

```text
WikiANN Turkish NER, 20,000 training sentences, identical recipe

model                     span P  span R  span F1   macro   train s   infer s
BERTurk (monolingual)      91.49   92.35    91.92   91.82     476.6      10.3
mBERT  (multilingual)      92.25   93.27    92.76   92.67     537.5       8.8
```

**The multilingual model came out ahead, by 0.84 span F1.** That is the
opposite of what this section was set up to show, and it is worth working
through rather than explaining away — starting with what the number can carry.
Both rows are a single training run at a single seed, and this book has not
measured how much a different seed moves span F1 on this task
(@sec-sequence-labeling says the same of its own table). So we do not know
whether the 0.84-point gap is stable. The measurement this table is missing is
several seeds per row on the same data split, with a paired uncertainty
interval, and until it exists the defensible statement is that **this
experiment does not show which model is better; nor does it show that the two
are equivalent**. Everything below is about why a gap this small is
unsurprising rather than about who won.

### First, the comparison is fairer than it looks

The obvious objection is size — mBERT has 177.3M parameters against BERTurk's
110.0M. But look at where the difference is:

```text
model                    total    word-embedding table   everything else
BERTurk                 110.0M                  24.6M             85.5M
mBERT                   177.3M                  91.8M             85.5M
```

("Everything else" is the twelve transformer layers plus the small position
embeddings and the tagging head; the word-embedding table is vocabulary size
× 768.)

[The transformer bodies are identical.]{.hl} Twelve layers, same width, same
85.5M parameters doing the actual computation. Almost all of the difference is
the embedding table, which is a lookup indexed by vocabulary size — 32,000
entries against 119,547. So mBERT is a bigger model in total: the embedding
table is real parameters, with real memory and update cost. But the encoder
bodies have the same capacity; the difference is a larger dictionary. Measure
memory and inference cost separately.

And it comes out ahead **despite** a tokenizer that splits Turkish into more
pieces, measured on the same test set:

```text
model                     vocab    subwords/word   mean sequence length
BERTurk                  32,000             1.66                   14.5
mBERT                   119,547             1.97                   16.8
```

mBERT produces about 19% more subwords per word on the same Turkish text (the
mean sequence length differs by about 16%), with a vocabulary 3.7× larger —
because most of that vocabulary belongs to other languages. The number of
pieces matters for compute and context budget; its effect on task accuracy
cannot be read off these numbers alone.

### Second, a confound that could explain it

**WikiANN is built from Wikipedia, and both models saw Wikipedia — in very
different proportions.**

mBERT was pretrained on Wikipedia alone, in 104 languages. BERTurk's 35 GB
corpus is a filtered OSCAR dump plus OPUS corpora plus a Wikipedia dump plus a
corpus contributed by Kemal Oflazer, so Wikipedia is only one part of its
training data rather than all of it (BERTurk's documentation does not give the
share as a number). The domain match is therefore a difference of degree
rather than of kind. That is a possible explanation of the 0.84-point gap, but
with one seed and uncontrolled pretraining differences between the two models
it cannot be confirmed. Even if more seeds showed the gap to be stable,
isolating the cause would take a separate experiment.

[The honest reading is therefore not "multilingual models are better for
Turkish".]{.hl} It is: *on a Wikipedia-derived task, the model whose pretraining
was entirely Wikipedia edged ahead by 0.84 points from one seed, despite
splitting the language into more pieces — and one seed cannot tell that from noise.*

### So what this section actually gives you is a protocol

There is no general verdict here. What there is, is a decision procedure —
four measurements. This order makes sense because the first two are cheap and
can help narrow the candidates:

1. **Fertility on *your* text.** Tokens per word for each candidate, on your
   own domain. Convert to cost and to effective context length
   (@sec-pretraining). This is usually a relatively cheap measurement.
2. **Domain overlap.** What was each model pretrained on, and how close is it
   to your data? The measurement above is an example of why this may matter,
   but it did not measure the effect separately.
3. **The task itself, both models, identical recipe.** The same training
   data, an equal tuning budget for each model (the same hyper-parameters may
   not suit both models equally), and the same set of several seeds.
4. **The operational columns.** Training time, inference latency, memory and
   cost under real load. Here, in a single run, mBERT trained 13% slower and — despite longer sequences — ran inference
   slightly faster, which is a reminder to measure rather than reason about
   throughput.

@rust2021good is the systematic version of this question: how much of the
monolingual advantage is the tokenizer rather than the model. Their answer,
across languages, is *a lot of it* — which makes step 1 the right place to
start.

::: {.column-margin}
Note what the result does *not* undermine. On this test set mBERT still splits
Turkish into about 19% more pieces per word, a tax on compute and context that
an accuracy number does not remove. But that 19% is a measurement of how the
two encoders split this NER data. To estimate the bill or effective context of
a generative model billed per token, measure the product's actual tokenizer and
its total input and output tokens on the same content.
:::

## Intuition checks {#sec-turkish-nlp-intuition}

Answer each one before you open it. All six are questions this chapter settled
with a measurement rather than an argument.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Your Turkish search box returns nothing useful. Where do you look first?

First sample real queries that failed, and compare tokenization, lowercasing,
apostrophe handling and stemming on the query side and the document side.
Whether you are indexing surface forms is one of the first places to look;
the index, the language setting and the relevance labels are candidates too.

This chapter's measurement used 7,165 Turkish documents and three-term queries
derived from the target sentence, with terms deliberately inflected differently
from the documents: surface-form BM25 gets **28.0%** recall@1, Snowball
stemming gets **95.3%**. When the query form differs from the document form,
exact matching cannot find that term; but measure the rate again on your own
usage.

If you have no Turkish stemmer, character 4-grams get 74.9% at 3.5× the terms
per document, and truncating to five characters gets 74.6% with no increase in
terms per document.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Why is `text.lower()` a correctness bug rather than a style choice?

Two reasons, and the second is worse.

Turkish has four letters where English has two — `İ i I ı` — and the case
mapping is not the ASCII one. Every token containing `I` or `İ` lowercases
differently under the two mappings — that follows from the mappings themselves
— and on the WMT16 Turkish source those 438 tokens are **0.95%** of all
tokens, many of them names. A different string is not a task error for every
token; measure the real error rate with your tokenizer on your task.

Then: `'İSTANBUL'.lower()` produces `i` followed by `U+0307 COMBINING DOT
ABOVE`, which is a nonspacing mark and not a word character. So with Python's
`re` module, `re.findall(r"\w+", ...)` returns `['i', 'stanbul']` — the word is split in
two, and NFC normalization does not put it back. The model never sees
`istanbul` at all.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Should you strip Turkish diacritics so `guzel` matches `güzel`?

Only with your eyes open. On the WMT16 source it merges 15,173 forms into
15,101 (a net loss of 72 forms; the ASCII keys merging at least two forms
also number 72) — just **72 collisions** — which looks like a free win until
you read them: *oldu* / *öldü* is "it happened" / "someone died". *bas* / *baş* is "press" /
"head".

The danger of that trade is that it can be too rare to show up in an
aggregate metric while some of the merged pairs change the meaning. Report
which original forms merge and their token frequencies, and check the
meaning-changing pairs in context, since context resolves some of them.
Restore the
diacritics if you can afford it. If you must strip, strip both sides and
document that those pairs are now indistinguishable.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. How much bigger is a Turkish vocabulary, really?

On identical content — 9,007 professionally translated sentence pairs —
Turkish produced **32,866 distinct forms from 141,412 tokens** against
English's **16,652 from 182,429**. Twice the vocabulary from 78% of the
tokens.

On equal-token prefixes the ratio rises from 1.49 at 5,000 tokens to 2.31 at
141,000 (equal-token prefixes do not cover the same sentences). Both curves
keep growing over this range; the Heaps exponent, roughly estimated from six
points, is about 0.78 for Turkish against 0.65 for English (no uncertainty
reported). A likely reason is that Turkish builds forms with suffixes. This is
an observation about the chosen range of this news corpus; it was not shown
that the ratio keeps widening as the corpus grows, so measure the curve again
for another domain or more data. Still, any design that assumes a vocabulary
can be enumerated — a fixed word list, a closed feature set, an exact-match
index — will strain against this growth.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. A colleague reports a Turkish benchmark score of 85. What do you ask?

First: 85 on which metric, which task, which test set, and which version?
Without that, nobody can say whether 85 is good or bad. Then three questions,
in order.

**Was the benchmark written in Turkish or translated into it?** A translated
benchmark measures the task through translationese, whose linguistic
properties can differ from text written in Turkish.

**Is the test set in the training set?** @sec-sequence-labeling found 13.06%
of a widely-used Turkish NER benchmark's test set verbatim in its own
training split. Hashing for exact overlap takes a few lines; check label
agreement and near-duplicates separately.

**What did the tokenizer do?** @sec-summarization found that the default
tokenizer of the widely used `rouge-score` implementation split 44.4% of the
words in 300 Turkish references at Turkish letters. If the score came out of a
tool that was validated on English, treat it as a hypothesis until the scorer
has been tested on Turkish control inputs.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. When is a multilingual model the right choice for Turkish?

When you need one deployment for many languages, when you need cross-lingual
transfer from a language with more labelled data, or when no monolingual model
exists for your language.

What you give up is measurable rather than mysterious: a multilingual
tokenizer may spend more tokens per Turkish word — here mBERT produced about
19% more subwords, but the rate is not the same for every multilingual
tokenizer, so measure it on your own text. Extra tokens cost money and context
(@sec-pretraining), and it spends vocabulary on languages you are not using.

But do not assume the accuracy follows. @sec-turkish-nlp-decide ran both on
the same task and **in a single run the multilingual one was 0.84 span F1
ahead**, despite producing 19% more subwords per word —
on a benchmark whose domain matched its pretraining corpus, from a single seed.
Measure fertility first, domain second, and the task third; and run more than
one seed before you call a gap that size a result.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-turkish-nlp-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.** The questions here
are not attributed to any company and are offered as topic exercises; the
numbers in the answers are this chapter's own measurements.
:::

### Testing whether you understand the language

**Q: Explain the Turkish `i` problem to someone who has never seen it.**

Turkish has four letters where English has two: dotted `i`/`İ` and dotless
`ı`/`I`. They are different letters, not different cases of one letter, so the
mapping between them is not the ASCII one — `I` lowercases to `ı`, and `i`
uppercases to `İ`. The consequence is the part interviewers are listening for:
`str.lower()` is not a style choice in Turkish, it is a **correctness bug**. It
turns `IŞIK` into `işik` where Turkish requires `ışık`. That every word
containing one of these letters comes out differently is guaranteed by the two
mappings; the measured number is how often such words occur — about one token
in a hundred on WMT16 news, concentrated in names and sentence-initial words.
It fails a second way too:
`'İstanbul'.lower()` returns `i` plus a *combining dot above*, nine code points
where `istanbul` has eight, so the two compare unequal while rendering
identically on screen — and a `\w+` tokenizer then splits it into
`['i', 'stanbul']`, which `NFC` normalization does not repair. The fix is a
locale-aware lowercaser wherever you need to lowercase, including inside your
metric code. But for a cased model, or a task that uses capitalisation, do not
lowercase at all; keep the preprocessing policy the same as the model's
training setup.

**Q: Why do subword tokenizers struggle with Turkish, and what does it cost?**

Because agglutination generates word forms combinatorially rather than
listing them: one stem plus a stack of suffixes, so `arkadaş` appeared in
**39 distinct forms** in a single corpus. A tokenizer trained mostly on English
either lacks pieces for those suffixes or has pieces that do not always line up
with morpheme boundaries (the `im|iz` split in @sec-text-as-data-turkish). The cost
falls in three places: more tokens for the same text — money on a service
billed per token, memory and compute in an encoder; less content per context
window, which is capability; and a faster-growing vocabulary — on equal-token
prefixes this chapter measured the Turkish/English type ratio *growing* from
**1.49** at 5,000 tokens to **2.31** at 141,000, with English flattening faster
over this corpus range. Measure the effect per task and per model, as tokens
per word and in total.

**Q: Stemming or morphological analysis for Turkish?**

For lexical retrieval, keep surface forms as the baseline and compare the
stemmer, an analyser and character n-grams on the same real query set.
Snowball is crude, over-merges and under-merges, and still took recall@1 from
**28.0% to 95.3%** on this chapter's queries, which were derived from the
target sentence with high inflection differences — a 3.4× improvement from one
preprocessing step, no model involved. Reach for a real morphological analyser when you need
the analysis itself rather than a matching key: recovering case to decide who
did what to whom, disambiguating `yüzü` (her face / the face / the hundred), or generating
forms. The engineering answer is that the cheap stemmer is a good first
candidate for retrieval, but may not be the first choice where explainability
or the cost of false matches is high; use an analyser when the grammatical
analysis is the output or the root/suffix split is required.

### Testing whether you have shipped something

**Q: You inherit a Turkish NLP system with no tests. What do you do first?**

Not train anything. Run the controls, because this chapter's whole argument is
that tools fail *silently* outside English. Lowercase a list of words with I
and İ and diff it against a correct lowercaser. For each metric, first write
down the value its definition predicts — identical candidate and reference, an
empty output, a one-character change — then feed it those. A perfect score on
identical input is expected for most metrics but not guaranteed for all
(aggregation, penalties or empty-example rules can differ). A copy of the
reference catches a harness that processes the two sides differently, like
the faithfulness proxy of mine whose first version also flagged copied text
(@sec-summarization). It does *not* catch a tokenizer that damages both sides
the same way: `rouge-score`, whose tokenizer splits 44.4% of the words in 300
Turkish references, still gives a
Turkish reference a perfect score against itself. For that, score two
sentences that differ in one Turkish word, or compare against a second
implementation, and print the tokens — on *güzel* against *özel*, which share
no word, `rouge-score` reports a ROUGE-1 of 0.67 instead of 0. Investigate an
unexpected result in terms of the metric's definition, the preprocessing and
the data alignment. Then measure fertility on real production text. In this
book each of these controls found a real problem; how long they take depends
on the system.

**Q: How do you budget an LLM feature for Turkish?**

By measuring with the product's actual tokenizer on your own text, rather than
by translating an English estimate. Fertility (pieces per word) is a
diagnostic; what decides the bill is the total billed tokens and the service's
terms. Be careful converting fertility into a bill, because they are not the
same ratio. Fertility is tokens *per word*, and
Turkish says the same thing in fewer words — @sec-machine-translation measured
English needing 1.29× as many word tokens for identical content. Combine the
two and a 1.5–2× fertility ratio comes out at roughly 1.2–1.6× the *total*
tokens on matched content. Treat that only as an illustrative calculation, not a
measured invoice: the two ratios come from different samples, a product's bill
cannot be derived by multiplying them, and the bill also separates
input from output pricing, caching and retries. If you want the number, count
total tokens for both languages on one parallel sample.
The same total ratio shrinks the effective context window, which for some
features can bind harder than price. Then add that the choice of model moves
this number: the tokenizer is one of the main levers, and it is fixed at
pretraining time, so it is a procurement decision rather than something you
tune later. Output length, prompt, price and caching also move the bill.

**Q: Your Turkish benchmark shows 92. Do you trust it?**

Ask what the control says: what does a simple baseline score, and how far
does a second seed move the number? This chapter fine-tuned a monolingual and a
multilingual model on the same Turkish task and the multilingual one came out
ahead, **92.76** to **91.92** F1 from a single seed, against the folklore and
against my own expectation. The two share a transformer body of the same size,
but vocabulary, tokenizer, pretraining data and fine-tuning interact; the
cause of the gap is unclear, and separating them takes controlled experiments.
One task and one seed are not a verdict. What earns trust is a protocol: fertility measured on
your text, domain overlap checked, both models fine-tuned on your data, and a
contamination audit before any number is quoted.

## Lab: a Turkish evaluation suite you can trust {#sec-turkish-nlp-lab}

The point of this lab is not to rank models. It is to test that the scorers
used on Turkish tasks behave as expected, and to build a small, documented
evaluation set — on a language the tools were not validated on.

### Step 1 — write three tasks, in Turkish, yourself

Fifty items each. Classification, extraction, and something generative. Write
them in Turkish rather than translating from English, because a translated
suite measures the task through translationese. These fifty items are for
auditing the scorer and the labelling guideline; they are usually not enough
to rank systems, catch rare errors or give a confidence interval. Keep them
clear and unambiguous — here you are building a measuring instrument, not a
challenge set. For a shipping decision, then build a larger, independent test
set that represents real usage, and separate ambiguous or conflicting items
through agreement between annotators.

### Step 2 — validate the scorer before scoring anything

Feed each metric a **perfect prediction** and confirm it returns a perfect
score. Then feed it a copied input, an empty prediction, a prediction that
differs by one character, and a pair of sentences that differ in one whole
Turkish word. Write down what each *should* return before you run it.

This step is the whole lab — and the perfect-prediction check alone is not
enough. @sec-summarization found a standard metric mutilating 44.4% of Turkish
words, and that metric passes the perfect-prediction test: both sides are
split the same way, so a reference still matches itself exactly. What exposes
it is a pair with a known *non-perfect* answer (*güzel* against *özel* should
share no word, yet scores 0.67), a second implementation that disagrees, or
simply printing the tokens.

### Step 3 — check your own text for the two normalization bugs

Lowercase your suite and search for `U+0307`. Count words containing `İ` and
compare `str.lower()` against `tr_lower()` on each. If your suite already
contains the bug, every model you evaluate will be scored on damaged input.

### Step 4 — measure fertility and convert it to money

For each model you plan to test, tokens per Turkish word on your own text.
Multiply by your request volume. This number often decides the choice before
accuracy does.

### Step 5 — run three models, including one multilingual

A Turkish-specific model, a multilingual one, and an LLM. Report accuracy,
tokens per request, latency, and cost per thousand requests — four columns,
because the first one alone has never decided a deployment.

### Step 6 — audit for contamination

Hash your suite's items against anything you know about the models' training
data. You will usually not be able to check a pretraining corpus; say so
explicitly rather than leaving it implied.

### What to hand in

The four-column table, the scorer-validation log from step 2 with its
predicted-versus-actual column, and a paragraph naming which model you would
ship and what would change your mind.

## Exercises {#sec-turkish-nlp-exercises}

1. **Vocabulary growth in your language.** Take any professionally translated
   parallel corpus and plot distinct forms against tokens for both sides.
   Report the ratio at three corpus sizes and say whether it is widening.

2. **Break the lowercaser.** Find a Turkish word where `str.lower()` produces
   something `re.findall(r"\w+", ...)` splits in two. Print the code points.
   Then check whether the libraries in your own stack have the same problem.

3. **The retrieval fix, on your data.** Index a Turkish corpus with BM25 twice,
   surface forms and stems. Query with dictionary forms. Report recall@1 for
   both, and decide what your search box should do.

4. **The diacritic collision list.** Strip diacritics from a Turkish
   vocabulary and list every ascii form that now maps to two or more real
   words. Rank them by how badly the confusion would matter in your domain.

5. **Fertility to invoice.** Take a Turkish document and its English
   translation, tokenize both with the tokenizer your product actually uses,
   and convert the difference into a monthly bill at your request volume. Then
   do it with a Turkish-native tokenizer and report the difference
   (@sec-pretraining has the method).

6. **Audit a Turkish benchmark.** Pick one you would use. Check for
   translation artefacts, hash its test set against its training set, and run
   its scoring script on a perfect prediction to confirm it returns a perfect
   score — then on two Turkish sentences that differ in one word, because a
   tokenizer that damages both sides equally still passes the first check.
   Report what you find, including if the answer is "nothing wrong".

7. **The control habit.** Take any metric you rely on and feed it an input
   whose correct answer you know for certain — identical strings, a copied
   document, an empty prediction. Write down what it should return and what it
   did. This exercise has a low hit rate and an enormous payoff.

## Where to go deeper {#sec-turkish-nlp-deeper}

Start by running `str.lower()` over a list of Turkish words containing I and
İ and diffing it against a locale-aware lowercaser. Everything else in this
chapter is downstream of believing that result.

| resource | what it is |
|:--|:--|
| [Zemberek](https://github.com/ahmetaa/zemberek-nlp) | the reference Turkish NLP toolkit — morphology, spelling, tokenization; the thing to reach for when a stemmer is not enough |
| [Mukayese](https://github.com/alisafaya/mukayese) | a Turkish benchmark suite with baselines; read what each task measures before quoting a score |
| [BERTurk](https://github.com/stefan-it/turkish-bert) | the monolingual models used here, with their corpora and training documented |
| [TDD — Türkçe Doğal Dil İşleme](https://tdd.ai/) | Turkish corpora, models and tools collected in one place |
| [Speech and Language Processing](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/) — Jurafsky & Martin | free online; the "Words and Tokens" chapter covers morphemes and subword tokenization. The finite-state treatment of morphology is in the printed second edition, not in this draft |

## What to remember {#sec-turkish-nlp-summary}

- **Agglutination is measurable, and it compounds.** On identical content,
  Turkish produced **32,866 distinct forms from 141,412 tokens** against
  English's **16,652 from 182,429** — twice the vocabulary from 78% of the
  tokens. The ratio grows with corpus size (1.49 → 2.31): both curves follow
  Heaps' law, but Turkish has the larger exponent (≈0.78 vs ≈0.65), because it
  generates forms by rule rather than drawing them from a list. Any design
  that assumes a vocabulary can be enumerated is fighting that.

- **`str.lower()` is a correctness bug in Turkish, twice over.** Every word
  containing `I` or `İ` comes out wrong under English rules — that part is
  arithmetic — and such words are about one token in a hundred (**0.95%** of
  the WMT16 source), concentrated in names. And `'İSTANBUL'.lower()` emits
  `i` plus a combining mark, so `\w+` returns `['i', 'stanbul']` — the word splits and NFC does not repair
  it. A three-line `tr_lower` before anything else touches the text.

- **Stemming is not optional in Turkish lexical search — on queries like the
  ones tested here.** Sixty-nine percent of that query set was built to differ
  from the document in inflection, so measure the gain on your own query logs
  before treating it as a requirement. Surface-form BM25: **28.0%** recall@1.
  Snowball stemming: **95.3%**. Character 4-grams get
  74.9% with no linguistic knowledge, at 3.5× the index. In English this is
  usually reported as a tweak; here it is whether the search box works.

- **Stripping diacritics causes only 72 collisions, and some of them are
  total.** *oldu* and *öldü* — "it happened" and "he died" — become the same
  string (a few, like *mi*/*mı*, cost nothing). Rare enough to pass every
  aggregate metric, severe enough to matter every time it hits.

- **A multilingual model came out ahead of the monolingual one on this task**, 92.76
  against 91.92 span F1 — with identical transformer bodies (85.5M each; the
  parameter gap is all embedding table) and *despite* tokenizing Turkish 19%
  worse — from a single seed, so not yet a separation. If the gap holds up,
  the likely reason is domain: the benchmark is built from Wikipedia and mBERT
  was pretrained on Wikipedia alone. There is no general verdict here,
  only a protocol — fertility on your text, domain overlap, both models on
  your task with an identical recipe, then the operational columns.

- **Subword tokenization replaced morphological analysis for modelling, not
  for everything.** Reach for a real analyser when the grammar is the output,
  when a wrong answer must be explainable, or when you need the stem to index
  on — and note that a stemmer of a few hundred lines carried most of the retrieval
  benefit.

- **The pattern, across five chapters: standard tools fail silently outside
  English.** `str.lower()`, `rouge-score`, BLEU, a benchmark's own splits, and
  a faithfulness proxy written for this book each produced a plausible wrong
  number on Turkish. None raised an error. Every one was caught by a **control
  measurement** — an input whose correct answer was known in advance — and none
  by reading the code. The last entry on that list is ours, which is the point:
  the failure mode is not other people's carelessness.

- **So build the control first.** Before trusting a tool on your language,
  give it something whose answer cannot be in doubt: identical strings, copied
  text, a perfect prediction, two texts that share no word, a majority-class
  floor. A perfect score on identical inputs is necessary, not sufficient — it
  cannot see a tokenizer that damages both sides alike. Ten minutes, and it is
  the highest-return ten minutes in a non-English NLP project.
